title: A weekend story

prepTasks.word: At the end of the evening,

writingModel: I want to tell you about one particular moment from last weekend — a moment I will never forget. It was Saturday evening, and four of us had gathered in Yerlan's dormitory room for dinner. Nobody planned it as a big event. Yerlan just invited us, said he wanted to cook, and we all arrived at seven o'clock with nothing but good moods and empty stomachs.

When I opened the door, the smell hit me immediately — rice, chicken, and spices, all cooked together in Yerlan's small electric pot. He stood at his desk, which he had transformed into a kitchen counter, stirring something with a wooden spoon. He looked completely focused, like a professional chef. Aisha was arranging a salad in a bowl. I sliced the bread and placed it on the table. We worked together quietly, and the room felt warm and full of life.

We sat down to eat at half past seven. Yerlan served the rice and we all tasted it at the same time. The silence lasted about three seconds. Then Saule said: "Yerlan. This is incredible." And she was right — it was the best home-cooked meal any of us had eaten since leaving our families. We talked about our hometowns, our grandmothers' cooking, our favourite foods from childhood. I told them about my mother's besbarmak. Aisha described her grandmother's samsa. Bekzhan mentioned his father's shashlik. Yerlan smiled and said: "Next time, we each cook something from home."

After dinner, Yerlan connected his laptop to a small speaker and searched for a film. We all suggested different ones — an action film, a romance, a documentary — but in the end we voted for a Kazakh comedy from 2019. Nobody remembered the title, but we all recognised the main actor. The film started, and for ninety minutes the room filled with laughter. The funniest moment was near the end — Saule laughed so hard at one scene that she knocked over her cup of tea. It landed on Aisha's notebook. Aisha screamed. Saule apologised. Then we all laughed even harder.

At the end of the evening, we washed the dishes together, folded the table back against the wall, and said our goodnights. I walked back to my dormitory alone through the quiet, dark corridor. The building was almost silent. But inside, I carried something warm — the kind of feeling you get when you realise that a place has started to feel like home. It was just dinner. Just four students in a small room. But it was the moment I understood: Uralsk, this city I moved to knowing nobody, had become my home. And these people — Yerlan, Saule, Aisha — had become my family.
